title: Spatial Configuration, Organisational Change and Academic Networks
research_question: This paper analyses the relationship between spatial configuration, organisational change and collaboration networks of academics by investigating results from an empirical case study of a single academic department at three points in time. In detail it analyses whether organisational cultures and academic life in the organisation remained relatively stable over time; whether interaction patterns significantly changed from one point in time to another as a result of these spatial and organisational changes; and how the networks of individual people transformed over time as a result of their personal careers and academic development, but also as people worked within different spatial settings at different points in time.

participants.description: Staff members of an interdisciplinary and research-intensive university department based in London / UK. The department size varied from 69 (2005) to 63 (2008) to 58 (2012) staff. A total of thirteen individual people were working for the department at all three points in time.
participants.recruitment: Network questionnaires were issued to all staff. Return rates were 65% (2005), 73% (2008), and 64% (2012).

stimuli_or_exposures.description: The department occupied different physical spaces at three points in time: 1) 2005: part of three floors of a large university building (1083sqm), mostly cellular offices. 2) 2008: same building, but refurbishment introduced a staff/student common room/kitchen/print room, some office moves. 3) 2012: completely new building across campus (1146sqm), occupying two adjacent floors (ground and lower ground), with increased open-plan space (31% of staff) and almost no single offices (2% of staff).

measures.instrument: Space Syntax (Visual Graph Analysis, Depthmap software) metrics: Mean Depth (MD)
Network questionnaire (3-point Likert scale: 1=useful, 3=extremely useful, summed score 6-9 for high usefulness)

measures.construct: Network structure (density, E-I index, ego network size, ego betweenness, homophily)
Space usage patterns and satisfaction with the building
Organizational metrics (department size, staff turnover, research groups, roles, gender)

findings.antecedent: Time period (2005, 2008, 2012) and associated spatial/organizational changes (e.g., increased accessibility, more shared offices)
findings.consequent: Average frequency of face-to-face contact for the whole department
findings.mechanism: Average accessibility increased (mean depth decreased from 9.282 to 5.857), and the number of people sharing offices increased, facilitating more contact.
findings.quote: The average frequency of face-to-face contact for the whole department increased from 2.06 (2005) to 2.66 (2008) and 2.77 (2012)

findings.antecedent: Time period (2005, 2008, 2012) and associated spatial/organizational changes (e.g., increased visibility, organizational events)
findings.consequent: Average perceived usefulness of colleagues for the whole department
findings.mechanism: Increasing levels of visibility (decreasing mean depth from 6.674 to 4.766) could have provided increased awareness of colleagues and their work. Managerial activities and joint organizational events also contributed.
findings.quote: average usefulness, which rose from 1.55 to 1.89 and 1.95.

findings.antecedent: Time period (2005, 2008, 2012) and associated spatial/organizational changes (e.g., common room introduction, then decentralization)
findings.consequent: Density of weekly face-to-face interaction network (freq345)
findings.mechanism: The introduction of a single common room/kitchen/print room in 2008 increased weekly interaction density. In 2012, providing a kitchen/print room on each floor decentralized meeting points, leading to a decrease in density.
findings.quote: density of the weekly interaction network first increased from 0.178 (2005) to 0.231 (2008), but then fell to 0.175 (2012).

findings.antecedent: Time period (2005, 2008, 2012) and associated spatial/organizational changes (e.g., increased visibility, organizational events)
findings.consequent: Density of high usefulness network (cumuseGT5)
findings.mechanism: Increasing levels of visibility (decreasing mean depth) could have increased awareness of colleagues. Managerial activities and joint organizational events also contributed.
findings.quote: density of the network of highly useful colleagues (0.037 → 0.040 → 0.047)

findings.antecedent: Time period (2005, 2008, 2012) and associated spatial/organizational changes (e.g., new staff, reduced research groups)
findings.consequent: Densities of overall contact network (freq12345) and overall usefulness network (cumuse)
findings.mechanism: Higher numbers of young and new staff in 2012 (less widely known) and reduction in separate research groups led to more selective, intensive interaction with fewer people.
findings.quote: The fact that the densities of the overall networks of contact and usefulness (...) continuously decreased over the years while averages of frequency of contact and usefulness increased can only be explained by a more selective interaction and collaboration behaviour

findings.antecedent: Department layout and organizational structure in 2008 (with common room)
findings.consequent: Daily face-to-face contact network structure
findings.mechanism: The introduction of a common room helped people across different groups to meet, leading to more balanced connections and more ties across group boundaries, despite similar network density to 2005.
findings.quote: In 2008, the density of the daily face-to-face interaction network remained almost the same. The structures were very different

findings.antecedent: Department layout and organizational structure in 2012 (new building, more open-plan, two kitchens, group D on lower ground floor)
findings.consequent: Daily face-to-face contact network structure
findings.mechanism: Fewer isolates and a single component emerged, but cohesion became uneven due to disjointed accommodation of groups on different floors (e.g., green group) and high cohesion in group/open-plan offices (red group).
findings.quote: In 2012, the network consisted of fewer isolates and only one single component. However, network cohesion became rather uneven

findings.antecedent: Organizational change (more events taking place, increasing opportunities for researchers from different groups to mix)
findings.consequent: Percentage of group internal ties in weekly interaction network
findings.mechanism: More events increased opportunities for researchers from different groups to mix, reducing the proportion of weekly interaction ties within groups.
findings.quote: Organisational reasons might be at the heart of the decrease of group internal ties from 47% in 2008 to 37% in 2012

findings.antecedent: Co-location on the same floor
findings.consequent: Percentage of floor internal ties in daily face-to-face interaction network
findings.mechanism: Proximity on the same floor consistently facilitates daily face-to-face interaction.
findings.quote: being on the same floor is a very strong determinant of who someone saw across all three points in time with percentages ranging from 86% to 91%.

findings.antecedent: Administrators' location on lower ground floor (2012)
findings.consequent: Administrators' average frequency of being seen face-to-face
findings.mechanism: Being located on a different floor cut off administrators from others based on the ground floor, reducing their visibility and contact frequency.
findings.quote: in 2012 almost half of them were located on the lower ground floor, which affected their frequency of being seen face-to-face.

findings.antecedent: Senior academic staff working from elsewhere (2012) after giving up single offices
findings.consequent: Senior academic staff average frequency of contact
findings.mechanism: Deliberate absence from the office and working remotely reduced face-to-face contact for senior staff.
findings.quote: their decreasing levels of contact might also be caused by the deliberate absence and working from elsewhere in 2012, after they had given up the solitude of their single offices.

findings.antecedent: PhD students allocated a large and very central area in the new building (2012)
findings.consequent: PhD students' average contact frequency and visibility
findings.mechanism: A central and large allocation in the new building increased their visibility and opportunities for contact with others.
findings.quote: PhD students: they were allocated a large and very central area in the new building in 2012 and thus their contact frequency and visibility to everyone else increased.

findings.antecedent: Role: Administrator
findings.consequent: Average frequency of contact and average perceived usefulness
findings.mechanism: Administrators consistently played a central role in bridging between groups, making them frequently seen and useful.
findings.quote: Administrators (marked in grey) were clearly seen most often and found most useful in all three studies.

findings.antecedent: Research Group D accommodated completely on lower ground floor (2012)
findings.consequent: Research Group D average frequency of contact
findings.mechanism: Being cut off from others based on the ground floor significantly reduced their visibility and contact frequency.
findings.quote: Group D is the only group accommodated completely on the lower ground floor of the new building, which cut them off significantly from others based on the ground floor.

findings.antecedent: Research Group D accommodated completely on lower ground floor (2012)
findings.consequent: Research Group D average perceived usefulness
findings.mechanism: Despite reduced contact frequency due to spatial separation, their value to others remained high.
findings.quote: this did not affect their value to everyone else, since members of group D were still found highly useful

findings.antecedent: Organizational change: closest colleagues of Research Group C leaving the department
findings.consequent: Research Group C average perceived usefulness
findings.mechanism: The weakening of the group due to the departure of key collaborators led to lower perceived usefulness.
findings.quote: group C behaved against the trend and showed lower values of average usefulness than everyone else. This might be rooted in the weakening of the group

findings.antecedent: Organizational restructuring of the department (2012), affecting Research Group C
findings.consequent: Internal network of high usefulness for Research Group C
findings.mechanism: The organizational restructuring, which most affected Group C, led to more isolates and a core structure of collaborative ties in dyads or triplets, indicating reduced internal collaboration.
findings.quote: structure of the group in 2012, which changed to more isolates and a core structure of collaborative ties in dyads or triplets.

findings.antecedent: Organizational change: end of large research project (between 2005-2008) for Research Group B
findings.consequent: Internal network of high usefulness for Research Group B
findings.mechanism: The conclusion of a large project dissolved clique-like mutual usefulness patterns, leading to a more star-shaped and hierarchical network structure.
findings.quote: clique-like mutual usefulness patterns in 2005 dissolved to a degree and became more star-shaped and hierarchical in 2008.

findings.antecedent: Organizational change: new externally funded research projects (2012) for Research Group B AND Spatial change: almost everyone in Group B moved to open-plan offices (2012)
findings.consequent: Internal network of high usefulness for Research Group B
findings.mechanism: New research projects fostered collaboration, and the shift to open-plan offices for most members (including senior staff) supported easier interaction and stronger bonds.
findings.quote: two externally funded research projects made the group connected in a more equal fashion again. The shift from 2008 to 2012 was supported by spatial changes

findings.antecedent: Role: Seniority (Professor, Senior Lecturer)
findings.consequent: Ego network size, heterophily, and betweenness centrality
findings.mechanism: More senior people tend to have broader roles and responsibilities, leading to larger, more diverse networks and a more central bridging position.
findings.quote: The more senior people tend to have larger and more heterophilic networks. They also tend to be more central in their own ego networks

findings.antecedent: Career advancement
findings.consequent: Ego network size
findings.mechanism: As academics advance, they establish their own agendas, research topics, reputation, and networks, leading to network growth.
findings.quote: As academics advance in their career, ego networks grow: for instance the network of person E grew from 6 to 9 to 8.

findings.antecedent: Career advancement
findings.consequent: Ego network homophily
findings.mechanism: With career advancement, academics take on different and multiple roles, diversifying their networks beyond their immediate group.
findings.quote: Ego networks also diversify with career advancement, for instance network homophily decreased for person D from 75% in 2005 to 40% in 2012, or for person E from 100% to 38%.

findings.antecedent: Organizational change: departure of colleagues from Research Groups C, D, E to a newly founded institute
findings.consequent: Ego network size (within the department) for persons C, D, E
findings.mechanism: The loss of important collaborators directly reduced the size of individuals' networks within the department.
findings.quote: The departure of important colleagues and collaborators... clearly left its mark in the networks of all three individuals of the associated group

findings.antecedent: Office type (single, double, group, open-plan) or location (accessibility)
findings.consequent: Structure of ego-networks
findings.mechanism: At the individual level, personal identity, character, and habits, along with career development, appear to be stronger drivers of ego network structure than specific spatial conditions.
findings.quote: space did not play a major role for the structure of ego-networks. Neither office type nor location (as measured by accessibility) seems to display any single pattern.

mechanisms: Spatial proximity and co-location facilitate face-to-face interaction and network tie formation.
Centralized common spaces (e.g., common room) act as social hubs, increasing encounter frequency and network cohesion.
Decentralized common spaces (e.g., multiple kitchens) can reduce overall network cohesion by dispersing interaction opportunities.
Increased spatial accessibility and visibility enhance awareness of colleagues and their work, potentially increasing perceived usefulness.
Organizational events and managerial activities can foster interaction and perceived usefulness across groups.
Staff turnover, especially of new or young members, can reduce overall network density as new members are less widely known.
Organizational restructuring, such as changes in research group composition or members leaving, directly impacts group and individual collaboration networks.
Seniority and career advancement lead to larger, more heterophilic, and more central ego networks due to broader roles and established reputations.
Individual identity, character, and habits play a significant role in shaping ego networks, potentially overriding direct spatial influences at the individual level.
Space acts as a mechanism for managing proximity and distance, bringing people together or keeping them apart, thereby shaping collective behaviors and network patterns.
implementation_implications: The findings on spatial configuration, organizational change, and collaboration networks in academic institutions may be transferable to other knowledge-intensive organizations.

Future research should combine traditional intra-organizational network studies with other academic network analyses (e.g., co-authorship, citation, social media) to understand how networks reach beyond departments.
Future studies should embed spatial configurations across different spatialities (physical and virtual space) to gain deeper insights into academic collaboration and peer production.

tables.description: Overview of minimum, average and maximum mean depth figures for visibility and accessibility models of the spatial network of the department in 2005, 2008 and 2012
Average figures of frequency of being seen and perceived usefulness for all staff as well as network densities of the department in 2005, 2008 and 2012
Overview of E-I index calculation results of weekly and daily interaction networks in 2005, 2008 and 2012 using both research group affiliation and floor of office location as category
Spatial information and metrics as well as network metrics of the ego networks of six selected academics over the years

limitations: The case study design, with significant changes in both spatial and organizational variables between the three time points, made it difficult to draw conclusive results on the distinct roles of space and organization in shaping academic collaborative networks.

The social network survey did not include members of a newly founded institute to which some colleagues departed, potentially underestimating the actual network extent of affected individuals (e.g., Person C).

control_conditions: comparison of different spatial/organizational configurations within the same department over time

mechanism_chain.description: Spatial and organizational changes influence the physical proximity and opportunities for interaction among department members, which in turn affects the frequency of face-to-face contact.

steps.from_construct: spatial/organizational changes (e.g., increased accessibility, more shared offices)
steps.to_construct: changes in physical proximity and opportunities for interaction
